Because my position on art is that it does not.exist as an abstract, it exists as a product of the mind that created it. There are theories of art that suggest that artists don't create art, but more discover it, like a mathematician would discover a function or formula; that art exists in some way independently of the one who crafted it. This isn't a theory of art I prescribe to. Instead, I feel that art is intrinsically linked to its creator. We can freely discuss the concepts that a piece of art can prompt us to conceive, those things that people ascribe as their interpretation, but those concepts prompted by the piece are something that exists because of yourself, not something intrinsic to the piece, because the piece itself was created with intent. We can also freely discuss the artists intent, and that how well we feel the piece conveys that and what we feel they did to convey that and what else they could have done, in the form of critiquing the work. But this can only be done on the basis of assessing the work on its original design criteria and premise; something we can either attempt to discern ourselves, if we have no artist to check with, or something we can do if the artist confirms themselves what they were trying to convey. But my point is these are two SEPARATE ways of analysing and discussing art. We shouldn't conflate the interpretations we have of unrelated topics thanks to to the influence of the piece, with some internal message of the piece itself. In other words, the perspective of the audience, is not invalid, but when discussing what art means, the positions are distinct from each other; one is internal to yourself, how the art makes you feel and think, and what the art does to bring that about within you, and another is abstract, based on what we think the message placed within a constructed piece is. If you believe art to be a product of its creator, then that message is intrinsically linked to the artist, their wills and desires, whether conscious or not. If you believe art exists independently of its creator; and this does not mean once it is created, but that the piece has some non-tangible existential existence that was extant before the creator brought the piece into being, then you can believe the piece.may have a deeper meaning or message the creator is unaware of. But this has its whole own set of philosophical problems.

My all means, I'm always happy to talk civilly about what is absolutely a nebulous question. Some would argue that those twins do have a right to kill their sibling. In fact, when conjoined twins are born, the seperation is often performed regardless of risk to a single baby. This is generally done because there is a much higher risk of complications in conjoined.twins who aren't seperated, but seperation almost inevitably goes ahead regardless. I'd say the bigger issue in this situation is often the question of whose body is it. Genetically those twins are, except in the rarest of rare cases, identical. The majority of non-identical cases end up as Chimerism, in that one fetus absorbs the other in utero, and potentially ends up with clusters of their cells in their body. For the identical ones, there's generally some level of greater integration of the shared bodyparts to one body over another, but they are, technically, a single human body comprised of two persons. They're actually really interesting cases that muddy the waters a bit, but for the purposes of this debate I'd say that if sufficient evidence could show which twin was medically dominant over the shared bodypart, that twin would have the right to have their twin removed. Not an easy decision to make by any means, but ethically justifiable. In regards to the severed arm, for me personally it comes back to my original point about potential life; the fetus isn't currently an independent life, and therefore doesn't deserve rights independent of its mother. However, it has a potential for independent life that a severed limb does not. It is that potential future that makes us place greater importance on the fetus. When it comes to the fusing thing, I'd again have to refer back to the twins assessment; if there was good medical evidence to support whose body it was, I believe they DO have a right to separate themselves, even if it kills the other person as a result. Unfortunately, this will always be an issue with no clear answer. Much of it boils down to ideas of humanity, personhood, and inherent value, and our own intrinsic beliefs in those areas dictate how we will consider the situation. As a person with a secular worldview, you will all life, especially human life, as sacred, and of inherent value. I'm an atheist, but for other reasons as well I hold that humanity has no intrinsic value, but that personhood is what gives our lives value, and that until a life form can exist independently of the vital systems of its host, that life form lacks an independent right to exist. It's not an easy topic, but my primary value in life is the intrinsic rights we grant humanity by virtue of their personhood, and my belief that those rights exist as far as they do not conflict with those of another. This in itself is a long topic of its own accord, in regards to how interactions between the rights of others infringe on your own, and vice versa, to what extent they should, and so on. A brief but by no means exhaustive summary would be to say that your right to life can compel me to inaction, so long as that life is not continuing on the basis of directly infringing one of my own. Your existence doesn't prevent me from killing you simply by virtue of you existing, but if it prevented me from exercising bodily autonomy, I would have the right to redress that to the extent that my right was returned.

In some respects I totally agree with you. But there are specific individual situations where I think applying the usual laws does a disservice to the creator, and I consider a famous cartoon mouse as one of them. I feel like there are situations in which the creator of the copywrited media has clear intentions for that media to be retained by the company they simultaneously created. I don't pretend to know anything about the vastly complex laws surrounding copywrite trademarks, intellectual property etc. But I know that at their core they're about protecting the rights of initial designers and creators of unique works, and their right to monetize that work for a prolonged period. Now for some things, like medicine or technology, where the work is more discovery than creation, it makes sense for that period of protected monetisation to be finite. But for artistic pieces that have become almost synonymous with the company they are owned by, or even represent, the idea that they could become public domain seems kinds silly to me. The idea that the company Walt Disney founded could lose their right to protect the legacy of Mickey Mouse, a legacy they have curated and are responsible for, seems wrong. Like Superman comics being made by Marvel, or Nintendo no longer holding onto Mario. But Coca-Cola can still protect their name, when many of these characters are as synonymous with their companies as their very names are.
